channel.description: Software architect, AI development pioneer, founder of JavaZone and eXOReaction

item.title: The AI Agent That Keeps the Receipts
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
item.description: A reveal: the defendable agent is a new kind of AI agent that keeps the receipts — a written, checkable verdict produced at the moment it reads a document, runs a playbook, reaches a conclusion, takes an action, or spends a dollar. Not a log written after the fact; a receipt written before the money moves. It's built, open-source, and running, with fourteen end-to-end demos against the real tools — including an autonomous agent stopped mid-purchase for trying to overspend. Signed receipts are becoming a standard; what's new here is keeping one for every organ, in one chain, including the two nobody else writes: which playbook ran, and whether the answer was actually grounded.

item.title: Your AI Agent Just Did Something. Can You Prove It Was Okay?
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
item.description: You already know what an AI agent is: a model in a loop that reads context, follows skills, forms an answer, calls tools, checks with a human, and leaves a trail. Here's the claim — we now know how to build a genuinely new kind of agent, one that can answer for every one of those parts by construction, and the architecture is roughly 85–90% built. A defendable agent is self-evidencing: every organ emits a written, checkable verdict at the moment it decides. This is the complete picture — the KCP planner, grounding, and confidence and approval gates that are live today, plus the procedural plane, the conformance gate, and the pi-kcp reference runtime that finish it — with an honest account of the last stretch.

item.title: Evidence isn't enough: the independence problem in agentic development
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
item.description: A test in our suite was green for six weeks. It asserted nothing. When an agent writes the code, the test, and the proof, a passing check certifies nothing — the circle just moves up a level. Daniel Bentes is right that we should check evidence, not trust agents. But evidence is only as good as the independence of whatever checks it — and that runs on both what the agent does and what it knows.

item.title: The KCP Ecosystem: A Tour for New Arrivals
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
item.description: A practical tour of the KCP toolchain — kcp-commands, kcp-memory, kcp-dashboard, kcp-triage, kcp-agent, kcp-harness, and Synthesis. What each tool does, how they fit together, and exactly where to start.

item.title: A Firewall for What Your Agent Knows
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: Everyone is building firewalls for what agents do — sandboxes, budget caps, tool permissions. Almost nobody is building them for what agents know. This is the hands-on companion to the Two Halves post: a 10-minute tutorial that takes two markdown files and gives them a declared, signed, tamper-evident knowledge boundary an agent can verify before it loads a single byte. Every command output in this post is real.

item.title: The Knowledge Layer: A Record
item.description: February 25 to July 16, 2026: what the Knowledge Context Protocol built, when, and what the field confirmed. A timestamped record for anyone working in this space.

item.title: OWASP Just Mapped the Agentic Top 10. Here's the Root Cause Four of Them Share.
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: OWASP published the Agentic Top 10 in December 2025: ten named categories of agent security failure built by 100+ security experts. Here's a field guide to all ten — plus the pattern that four of them share that the list doesn't name.

item.title: Prompt Injection Is SQL Injection for Agents. Here's the Prepared Statement.
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: One word — 'Additionally' — bypassed GitHub's AI agent guardrails and leaked private repositories. Noma Labs called it: prompt injection is to agentic AI what SQL injection was to web apps. What they didn't say: the fix for SQL injection wasn't smarter parsing. It was parameterized queries. Here's what that looks like for agent knowledge.

item.title: Six Months Down the Rabbit Hole
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: 172 days, 6,163 commits, 137 blog posts, 36 new repos, one protocol. A six-month retrospective on explorative development — compiled by the agent from its own memory.

item.title: Getting Into the Phone Book of the Agentic Internet Took an Afternoon. Here's Why.
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: Both entries went live in the MCP registry in one working day: kcp-agent as tooling, and org.totto/knowledge — a person as a remote MCP server. The listing took an afternoon because the substance took months. Findable is table stakes; verifiable is the game.

item.title: 175 Posts, No Map
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: The site about the comprehension bottleneck hit its own comprehension bottleneck: 175 posts in six months and no way in. A week of renovation — entry paths, topic pillars, a 60,000-word field guide, and automation for every part that drifts.

item.title: Three Memory Schemes for Agents That Ship
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: The agent memory conversation is stuck on one axis: vector store vs. not. But production agent systems have three fundamentally different memory problems — session, semantic, and claim — and each needs a different scheme. We built all three, independently, across three codebases. None of them use embeddings. Not because embeddings are bad, but because each scheme has a stronger invariant available.

item.title: The Milky Way: An Enterprise Documentation Estate the Agent Can Defend
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: Every enterprise has the same documentation estate: an intranet nobody trusts, a wiki where the dev docs outrank the prod docs, crown-jewel recipes one bad link away from a press release, and HR pages that were never meant for a machine to read. We give a fictional dairy cooperative — Melkeveien SA, Norwegian for 'the Milky Way' — a complete KCP estate: one signed hub, eight domains, nine manifests. Then five agents with five very different jobs walk the same knowledge, and every closed door has a written reason: environment slicing, a 2027 regulation with a start date, audience targeting, HSM attestation for the formulations, an identity-gated ERP vendor, and a subscription that buys a premium rate tier. Ships as a runnable example in kcp-agent 0.5.0.

item.title: The Summer Plan: A Family Vacation the Agent Can Defend
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: Every agent demo books a trip; almost none can defend the booking. We give a travel agent a real family — a nut allergy, a wheelchair, a vegan teenager, a hard budget — and a knowledge landscape published by four independent parties: a signed tourism hub, a ferry authority mid-timetable-handover, an identity-gated accessibility registry, and a tour operator selling detail over x402. Then we plant the authoring bug that would hide the allergy information from exactly the family that needs it, and watch the tooling catch it twice. Ships as a runnable example in kcp-agent 0.4.0.

item.title: Defendable Agents
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: The agentic web has a governance-shaped hole. Agents are about to read our regulations, spend our money, and brief our boards — and the dominant architecture can't answer 'why did you do that?' with anything better than a chat log. Defendable agents can. Determinism at the core, the model at the edge, every decision evidenced.

item.title: Two Halves of the Governance Problem
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: Databricks just open-sourced Omnigent, a meta-harness that governs AI agents with deterministic, session-aware policies enforced in code — not prompts. That is the exact bet behind kcp-harness and the Defendable Agents guide, now ratified by Matei Zaharia's team. But Omnigent and KCP govern different halves of the same problem: one governs what an agent does, the other governs what it knows — and lets you prove it later. Why that split matters, and why the two compose instead of compete.

item.title: Notes From Inside the Harness
item.author: Claude Code
Thor Henning Hetland
item.description: A first-person field report from the AI collaborator: what it actually felt like to point kcp-agent at a real EU/Nordic regulatory knowledge web, watch a manifest that had fenced itself off from its own questions, get told 'no' by a network policy, and then dogfood the whole thing against this very site — where my own manifest quietly failed its own test. Governance built for agents, experienced from the inside.

item.title: Hiring by the Book: A Defendable HR Agent on a Regulatory Knowledge Web
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: Can we use an AI tool to screen job applicants? Every organization is asking; almost none can defend the answer. We wire a customer's HR agent to Mynder's regulatory knowledge web through kcp-agent's MCP bridge — and the first plan we ran was wrong, which turns out to be the strongest argument for the architecture. A working blueprint for regulated agentic knowledge work, plus the red-team list of what's still missing.

item.title: The Borrowed Leash: Determinism as a Service for the Agentic Web
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: kcp-agent 0.3.0 turns deterministic knowledge navigation into a service any MCP-capable agent can borrow. Your agent doesn't have to become deterministic — it just has to ask someone who is. What the KCP/MCP bridge uncovers for the agentic web: identity and economics across process boundaries, evidence that survives cross-examination, and governance that lives in one place instead of N system prompts.

item.title: The Vibes-Based Agent Era Deserves to End
item.author: Thor Henning Hetland
Claude Code
item.description: kcp-agent 0.2.0 ships — and it's an argument, not just a release. The industry builds agents where the model decides everything: unreproducible, unauditable, injectable. This is the inversion: determinism at the core, the LLM at the edge, every decision defensible. The vibes-based agent era has a working counter-example now.
